paper_title: ProAR: Learning Prospective Reasoning with Autoregressive Video Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autoregressive (AR) video models excel at causal generation, but their reliance on next-chunk prediction confines them to a short-sighted, reactive paradigm. This limitation is particularly consequential for reasoning-oriented generation, where achieving a target outcome through valid intermediate states matters more than local visual plausibility. To address this challenge, we propose Learning Prospective Reasoning with Autoregressive Video Models (ProAR), a novel framework that transforms autoregressive video generation into a goal-oriented reasoning process. ProAR introduces two key components: (1) To anchor generation to the long-range outcome, we integrate goal-frame prediction into the autoregressive loop via an asymmetric attention mask, enabling the predicted goal frame to guide the generation of intermediate states without being disrupted by them. (2) To guide short-range transitions, we introduce future representation self-alignment to encourage current hidden states to anticipate upcoming temporal dynamics. By leveraging teacher-forcing in AR training, we extract clean future representations in a single forward pass and align current representations with them using a lightweight, training-only predictor. Together, these two mechanisms seamlessly combine explicit, sparse target supervision with implicit, dense step-wise guidance, promoting coherent, goal-directed reasoning progress with modest computational cost. Experiments show that ProAR's complementary components consistently improve performance across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks. The framework proves highly training-efficient, surpassing fully trained standard AR baselines using only 25% of the training steps. This paradigm also demonstrates promising applicability to embodied reasoning tasks.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Video generation models are moving beyond visual synthesis toward reasoning through visual dynamics. They have been used to solve game-like problems such as maze navigation and visual puzzles (Wang et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2026b; Zhu et al., 2026b), simulate physical processes (Yao et al., 2026), and support embodied control (Bruce et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026c; He et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). In these settings, the generated video is itself the reasoning process: the model must achieve target outcome by generating sequence of valid visual states. This paradigm requires video models to reason about and plan the evolution of visual states, rather than merely produce visually plausible content, opening new possibilities for physical and embodied intelligence (Kataoka et al., 2026). We refer to this emerging paradigm as video-native reasoning, where model reasons by directly generating how the visual world evolves. Autoregressive (AR) video models provide natural foundation for video-native reasoning. Unlike bidirectional video models, AR models generate video sequentially, conditioning each new chunk on the preceding visual history. This causal generation process supports long-horizon generation and low-latency streaming (Teng et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a), making AR models particularly suitable for real-time and interactive applications (Teng et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a). However, there is fundamental mismatch between the standard AR training objective and reasoning-oriented generation. Next-chunk prediction optimizes only for locally plausible continuations of the observed history without accounting for their impact on eventual task completion, influencing all subsequent predictions. Existing methods primarily focus on improving visual quality, temporal consistency, or prediction horizon (Yu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a; Qian et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026), rather than explicitly addressing the short-sightedness of AR generation in goal-directed reasoning tasks. We argue that autoregressive video-native reasoning requires prospective view of generation. We define prospective reasoning as the capacity to anticipate possible future outcomes and state transitions based on observed history, and to use this foresight to guide ongoing generation. This perspective exposes two complementary requirements (Fig. 1(b)). At the long-range level, the model should anticipate its target outcome. At the short-range level, it should anticipate upcoming transitions that drive meaningful progress. Long-range outcome awareness provides global direction, while shortrange transition awareness encourages coherent and steady progress toward the goal. Together, they enable future expectations to guide present generation, rather than solely reacting to the past. Motivated by these requirements, we propose Learning Prospective Reasoning with Autoregressive Video Models (ProAR). ProAR introduces two complementary mechanisms: (1) Outcome guidance provides explicit but sparse long-range supervision. At each autoregressive step, ProAR jointly predicts the current chunk and goal frame representing the anticipated final state. An asymmetric attention mask prevents the current chunk from influencing the goal belief, while allowing the predicted goal to guide current generation. As the video unfolds, the model continuously updates its goal belief based on the growing history. (2) Transition guidance provides implicit and dense shortrange supervision through future representation self-alignment. Leveraging teacher forcing, ProAR reuses the clean next-chunk representation computed within the same forward pass to supervise the current states to anticipate upcoming temporal dynamics. This design requires neither an external representation encoder nor an additional backbone forward pass, and the lightweight alignment predictor is removed entirely during inference. At inference, ProAR generates autoregressively without access to ground-truth future states, relying on its dynamically updated goal-frame predictions and learned anticipatory representations to guide generation. We evaluate ProAR on 13 visual reasoning tasks, including 10-task subset of VBVR (Wang et al., 2026a) covering perceptual and spatial reasoning, and 3 abstract reasoning tasks from VideoRLVR (Zhu et al., 2026b). Compared with standard AR generation, ProAR raises the mean score on the 10task VBVR subset from 0.663 to 0.801, and the average success rate on VideoRLVR from 50.97 to 52.97. Ablation studies further demonstrate that Outcome and Transition guidance provide complementary gains across these tasks. ProAR is also highly training-efficient: on the 10-task VBVR subset, it surpasses the fully trained AR baseline using only 25% of the training steps. Moreover, ProAR demonstrates promising generalization to embodied reasoning, delivering consistent improvements on the WorldArena simulation benchmark (Shang et al., 2026). Our contributions are threefold: (1) We revisit autoregressive video generation from reasoning perspective, identifying the lack of prospective guidance as key limitation of next-chunk prediction. (2) We propose ProAR, which combines goal belief and future representation self-alignment to provide outcome and transition guidance with minimal overhead. (3) Experiments across diverse video reasoning tasks demonstrate the complementary benefits of outcome and transition, driving consistent improvements in both reasoning performance and training efficiency, with promising generalization to embodied reasoning.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Autoregressive Video Generation. Autoregressive video models generate frames or chunks causally, making them suitable for long, streaming, and interactive generation. Recent methods improve scalability (Teng et al., 2025), efficiency (Yang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2026c), and training stability (Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a) during autoregressive rollout. Several studies have explored richer future information beyond next-chunk prediction through foresight alignment (Yu et al., 2026), hierarchical denoising (Qian et al., 2026), and futureaware training (Xu et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026). These advances have also enabled interactive world models and world action models for embodied agents (Bruce et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026c; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). However, extending the prediction horizon alone can improve visual quality, but is insufficient for task-oriented generation which requires both clear target and effective intermediate transitions. We address these needs with complementary outcome and transition guidance. Native Reasoning with Video Generation Models. Recent studies have begun to treat video generation as paradigm for reasoning rather than only visual synthesis (Tong et al., 2026; Wiedemer et al., 2025; He et al., 2026; Qi et al., 2026). Video generators can perform visual reasoning by generating intermediate solution steps, such as navigating maze or moving pieces to solve puzzle (Wang et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2026b). Existing approaches improve reasoning capabilities through visual prompting (Geirhos et al., 2026), test-time training (Cheng et al., 2026; Jun et al., 2026), explicit chains of visual thought (Huang et al., 2025), and reinforcement learning (Zhu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026b). Other studies further investigate how reasoning capabilities emerge in video generation models (Wang et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026a). However, most of these methods build on bidirectional generators that jointly denoise all frames and allow dense interactions across time. Autoregressive models instead strictly enforce causal generation, committing to each chunk without seeing future frames or revising past errors. The closest work in this setting (Qian et al., 2026) introduces hierarchical coarse-to-fine denoising for autoregressive video reasoning. In contrast, ProAR provides lightweight outcome and transition guidance without changing the basic chunk-wise generation process. Representation Learning in Diffusion Models. Diffusion models learn rich semantic and structural features in their intermediate layers (Tang et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2023). One line of work aligns generative representations with strong pretrained feature spaces (Oquab et al., 2023; He et al., 2022; Assran et al., 2023) to improve training efficiency and generation quality (Yu et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2026; Leng et al., 2025). Another line derives supervision from the generative model itself, using stronger internal representations to guide weaker ones (Jiang et al., 2025; Haghighi et al., 2026; Chefer et al., 2026). Recently, representation alignment has also been explored in video post-training (Zhang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026). Most relatedly, Video-Mirai (Yu et al., 2026) distills future bidirectional representations into autoregressive causal features but requires an additional forward pass. In contrast, our Transition module exploits autoregressive training properties to obtain clean future representations within the model, requiring neither an external representation encoder nor an additional model pass.

From Next-Chunk Prediction to Prospective Reasoning. Video-native reasoning requires each generated video to complete specified task. This imposes two requirements beyond visual plausibility: (1) goal completion, where the final state must satisfy the task objective, and (2) progression validity, where intermediate transitions must follow task logic or physical constraints. However, the local objective LAR (Eq. 2) supervises only the current chunk given its preceding history. It does not directly supervise whether the prediction supports the final objective or enables valid subsequent transitions. During inference, every generated chunk is appended to the history and cannot be revised, allowing early errors to persist and compound throughout the autoregressive rollout. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), locally plausible rollout may therefore culminate in task failure. This gap motivates prospective reasoning in Fig. 1(b): anticipating state evolution and future outcomes from available observations, then using these expectations to guide current generation. It requires guidance at two temporal scales. Long-range guidance maintains an expectation of the final outcome, while short-range guidance anticipates the next stage of progression. Joint prediction alone cannot guarantee the desired information flow. We therefore introduce an asymmetric attention mask (Fig. 2(b)). Specifically, goal tokens attend only to the clean history and themselves, shielded from the noisy current chunk. Conversely, current tokens additionally attend to these goal tokens. This target-first dependency prevents the uncertain current state from corrupting the goal belief, while allowing the anticipated goal to guide ongoing generation, modulated by the loss weight λgoal in Eq. 7. During inference, the model jointly denoises the current chunk and goal input, but only the generated current chunk is appended to the history. The goal belief is re-estimated at the next step from the expanded history, allowing it to be progressively refined as the video unfolds. 3.3 TRANSITION: REPRESENTATION ALIGNMENT FOR PROGRESSIVE REASONING Outcome guidance specifies where the generation should end, but leaves how the current state should evolve unconstrained. Transition guidance addresses progression validity by answering What should happen next? Our key intuition is that the current representation should anticipate the next stage of the task. We realize this intuition through future representation self-alignment. Teacher and Student. Recent studies show that intermediate hidden states of diffusion models encode rich semantic and temporal abstractions, and that stronger hidden states can guide weaker ones to improve generation (Jiang et al., 2025; Haghighi et al., 2026). Our core idea is to use the clean representation of the next chunk to guide the noisy representation of the current chunk, as illustrated in Fig. 2(c). The clean next-chunk hidden states contain uncontaminated information about the next stage and therefore serve as strong, prospective teacher. In contrast, the noisy current hidden states contain incomplete and noise-corrupted information, serving as the weaker student. (2) Autoregressive Models: We adapt the open-source Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Wan et al., 2025) backbone to autoregressive generation using causal attention and teacher-forcing training. This Standard AR baseline is trained and evaluated under the same settings as ProAR. Implementation Details. We optimize all models using AdamW with learning rate of 5 106 and global batch size of 16. The chunk size is 4 frames for VBVR and VideoRLVR, and 8 frames for WorldArena. We conduct every training on 2-4 NVIDIA B200 GPUs. For Outcome Guidance, the final ground-truth frame serves as the goal target. We set λgoal = 0.25 and λalign = 0.01 by default. Since the raw cosine alignment loss is much larger than the generation losses, the weighted alignment term contributes approximately 3%10% of the total loss. Transition guidance is activated in the later training stages: at step 7,500/10,000 for VBVR and step 3,000/5,000 for VideoRLVR. After Transition guidance is activated at step 7,500, the score further increases from 0.7666 to 0.8010 by step 10,000. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we present ProAR, novel framework that equips autoregressive video generation with prospective reasoning capability. To address the short-sightedness of next-chunk prediction, ProAR combines outcome guidance for goal completion with transition guidance for valid intermediate progression. Experiments across perceptual, spatial, abstract, and embodied reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements with modest computational overhead. These results highlight prospective modeling as promising direction for advancing video-native reasoning, opening new possibilities for physical and embodied intelligence.

sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: Video Configuration. In addition to the chunk settings detailed in the main paper, VBVR videos are generated at 512512 resolution with task-specific sequence lengths. VideoRLVR videos consist of 81 frames at 832 480 resolution. During inference, we employ 20 denoising steps per chunk. Further ablations on the configuration settings are detailed in Sec. A.2. WorldArena Settings. WorldArena (Shang et al., 2026) evaluates video world models as embodied simulators across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (Chen et al., 2025). Since the original trajectory lengths vary substantially, we follow the FlowWAM (Chen et al., 2026b) protocol to standardize the training data: each video is uniformly sampled to 121 frames and resized to 640 480 resolution. For evaluation, WorldArena introduces 1,000 newly generated test trajectories (20 per task) beyond the official RoboTwin dataset. Following WorldArenas default configuration, we generate these test videos in the identical 121-frame and 640 480 format. This ensures structural consistency between training and inference while preserving the complete physical manipulation process. Given these longer videos, we use chunk size of 8 and set λgoal = 0.25 and λalign = 0.05. We train for 10000 steps and start the transition module at step 7000. Computational Cost. ProAR introduces only modest computational overhead over Standard AR during both training and inference. Training: Outcome guidance appends one goal frame to each 4-frame chunk, increasing the token count by 8%11% for videos of 38 chunks. Transition guidance is highly efficient: it reuses internal representations from the same forward pass without requiring an external teacher. Its lightweight 3-block predictor (236M parameters, just 4.7% of the 5B backbone) adds mere 2%3% to the training computation. Overall, ProAR increases the total training cost by only 12%14%. Inference: The Transition predictor is discarded entirely, yielding zero overhead. Meanwhile, the Outcome module jointly denoises the goal frame alongside the current chunk without any additional forward passes or sampling steps. Measured on an NVIDIA B200 GPU, ProAR increases the overall inference time by approximately 12% for chunk size of 4 compared to standard AR generation. Since only single goal frame is added per step, this relative overhead diminishes further with larger chunk sizes. For example, generating 8-frame chunks in WorldArena incurs marginal time increase of only 8%. Moreover, the asymmetric attention pattern is sparser, making it more computationally efficient. We therefore use the asymmetric mask as the default Outcome configuration. Fig. 5 illustrates how Standard AR can fail either requirement: rollout may remain locally plausible but end without completing the task (Goal Failure), or produce invalid intermediate interactions that violate task rules (Rule Violation). In contrast, successful trajectory preserves valid transitions and reaches the intended goal. Red boxes highlight erroneous states, while green arrows indicate the successful path. Visualization of Future Representation Alignment. As described in Sec. 3.3, transition guidance injects prospective information into current hidden states. To examine this effect, we visualize the resulting representations. During teacher-forcing training, all video chunks are processed in parallel within single forward pass. For each transition from chunk to chunk + 1, we extract the noisy current hidden states from Layer 15 at moderate noise level (σ = 0.5). We then pass them through the trained lightweight DiT predictor to obtain the student prediction. The clean hidden

As shown in Fig. 6, the noisy current representations primarily reflect the spatial state of the current chunk. For VBVR (Wang et al., 2026a), task-specific rule-based evaluators assess the generated video against its reference solution and task objective. Depending on the task, they measure final-state correctness, object and spatial consistency, transition validity, and rule compliance. Each video receives continuous score in [0, 1], where higher value indicates greater task completion. This score should not be interpreted as binary success rate. For VideoRLVR (Zhu et al., 2026b), we report Precision, Recall, F1, and Success Rate (SR), macroaveraged over the test samples. F1 is the harmonic mean of the per-sample Precision and Recall. The task-specific metrics are defined as follows. For Maze, Precision and Recall measure the overlap between the generated and reference path regions, while SR requires connected path from start to goal without corrupting the maze walls. For FlowFree, Precision and Recall measure the color correctness and coverage of filled non-endpoint cells. SR additionally requires valid non-overlapping paths, preserved endpoints, correct color connectivity, and sufficient grid coverage. For Sokoban, Precision and Recall compare the generated and reference action sequences at corresponding steps. SR requires all boxes to reach their targets through sufficiently valid state transitions. Precision, Recall, and F1 measure local agreement with the reference solution, whereas SR evaluates strict task completion. Consequently, high F1 score does not necessarily imply high success rate. sections.content: IRASim. IRASim (Zhu et al., 2025) is an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer that predicts future robot observations from historical frames and action trajectories. Vidar. Vidar (Feng et al., 2025) combines large-scale multi-view video diffusion pretraining with masked inverse dynamics to infer robot actions from predicted visual trajectories. Genie Envisioner. Genie Envisioner (Liao et al., 2026) uses an instruction-conditioned video diffusion model for autoregressive robotic simulation and policy learning. Ctrl-World. Ctrl-World (Guo et al., 2026) combines joint multi-view prediction, framelevel action conditioning, and pose-conditioned memory retrieval to support controllable and temporally consistent rollouts. FlowWAM. FlowWAM (Chen et al., 2026b) represents actions as dense optical-flow videos and jointly models flow and RGB observations using dual-stream diffusion framework. Controlled Autoregressive Baseline. Standard AR. We adapt the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Wan et al., 2025) backbone to autoregressive generation using causal attention and teacher-forcing training. This serves as our Standard AR baseline and follows the same training and evaluation protocol as ProAR. Results. As shown in Table 10, ProAR achieves an EWMScore of 60.95, ranking first among the autoregressive models and second across all evaluated systems. More importantly, under the controlled comparison with standard AR, ProAR improves 13 of the 16 base metrics and raises EWMScore from 60.43 to 60.95. The gains span several task-relevant dimensions, including Depth Accuracy (88.42 to 91.11), Instruction Following (80.88 to 81.96), Background Consistency (87.10 to 88.11), Interaction Quality (73.12 to 73.86), and Trajectory Accuracy (41.74 to 42.34). These results indicate that prospective guidance improves not only visual consistency but also spatial accuracy, physical interaction, and task alignment, supporting the extension of ProAR from visual reasoning to embodied video simulation. A.6 LIMITATIONS AND DISCUSSIONS While ProAR establishes powerful paradigm for video-native reasoning, our current implementation of Outcome guidance relies on simple heuristic: utilizing the final video frame to represent the target outcome. This design choice is highly effective for most goal-oriented reasoning tasks, where the final frame naturally encapsulates the goal completion state. However, this rigid assumption introduces limitation. In scenarios where the final frame is semantically uninformative, such as tasks with post-completion idle states or purely process-driven dynamics, predicting this frame may provide weak supervision. Consequently, the model may struggle to extract meaningful long-range guidance. promising direction for future work is to transition from fixed final-frame target to adaptive milestone guidance. Rather than strictly anchoring to the last frame, future frameworks could dynamically detect the most salient keyframes or critical bottleneck states within the visual sequence, utilizing them as flexible goals or intermediate subgoals. This would further generalize prospective reasoning to more open-ended and complex physical environments.
